items.stem: For unstructured search over N items, roughly how many evaluations does Grover's algorithm need compared with a classical search?

options.text: About sqrt(N) versus about N classically - a quadratic speedup
options.rationale: Correct: Grover gives a quadratic speedup, needing on the order of sqrt(N) iterations.

options.text: About log(N) versus N - an exponential speedup
options.rationale: Grover is quadratic, not exponential; log(N) overstates the advantage.

options.text: About N versus N - no speedup at all
options.rationale: Grover does provide a quadratic advantage over classical search.

options.text: About N^2 - it is slower than classical search
options.rationale: Grover is faster, not slower, scaling as sqrt(N).

items.explanation: Correct: Grover gives a quadratic speedup, needing on the order of sqrt(N) iterations.

items.stem: Which TWO statements about Shor's algorithm are correct? (Select TWO.)

options.text: It can factor large integers efficiently, threatening RSA
options.rationale: Correct: Shor's algorithm factors integers in polynomial time, undermining RSA.

options.text: It relies on quantum period finding via the quantum Fourier transform
options.rationale: Correct: Shor reduces factoring to period finding, solved with the QFT and phase estimation.

options.text: It already runs on commercial noisy devices to break real keys
options.rationale: Fault-tolerant hardware at the needed scale does not yet exist.

options.text: It speeds up every optimisation problem exponentially
options.rationale: Shor targets factoring/discrete-log structure, not arbitrary optimisation.

items.explanation: Correct: Shor's algorithm factors integers in polynomial time, undermining RSA.

items.stem: Why is interference essential to quantum algorithms rather than simply 'trying all inputs at once'?

options.text: Interference is engineered so wrong answers cancel and the right answer's amplitude grows before measurement
options.rationale: Correct: algorithms arrange constructive/destructive interference so measurement is likely to yield the answer.

options.text: Because measurement returns all superposed answers simultaneously
options.rationale: Measurement returns one outcome; you cannot read all branches.

options.text: Because qubits store exponentially many classical results you can print out
options.rationale: You cannot extract all amplitudes; only measurement statistics are accessible.

options.text: Because interference copies the correct answer to every qubit
options.rationale: No-cloning forbids copying; interference reshapes amplitudes, it does not copy results.

items.explanation: Correct: algorithms arrange constructive/destructive interference so measurement is likely to yield the answer.
